overview: White develops the bishop to c4 instead of chasing the knight with e5, so 2...Nxe4 is possible and White can play 3.Bxf7+ (the Krejcik Gambit) Kxf7 4.Qh5+ for a king hunt that mostly just regains material with a loose Black king. Black can also play 2...d5 or 2...e6 and reach comfortable positions. It is mostly a surprise and trap line, not a main-line approach.

white_ideas.idea: 3.Bxf7+ Kxf7 4.Qh5+ and Qd5+ to win back the knight with the Black king exposed.
Develop quickly with Nc3, d3 or Qe2 and aim at f7.

black_ideas.idea: 2...Nxe4 and survive the king hunt with ...g6 and ...e6.

typical_structures.structure: Open game with exposed black king or a normal e4/d5 structure if Black plays 2...d5.

character.notes: Bxf7+ lines are a forced king hunt; both sides can go wrong quickly; low confidence.

gambit.notes: At the root nothing is offered; the 3.Bxf7+ sacrifice mostly regains material by force.

soundness.notes: Thought dubious as a way to claim advantage, since Black can defend; not quite refuted.

structure.notes: Open centre when e4 is taken; otherwise e4/d5 tension.

approach.notes: Strong players seldom choose it over 2.e5.

sublines_that_differ.name: Krejcik Gambit
sublines_that_differ.how: Forced king hunt; White regains the knight with a displaced Black king.

gambit.reason: Nothing offered at the root; the sacrifice comes back by force.

soundness.reason: A surprise attempt Black can meet well; not a mainstream try.

structure.reason: The e4 pawn goes and lines open.

level.reason: Forced lines to know; dubious, so never beginner.

plans.reason: The bishop aims at f7 from move two.
